content: Fluency, also referred to as volubility or loquaciousness, is a characteristic of an individual or a system that conveys information rapidly and with a high degree of expertise. This is exemplified by a very low average time between the generation of successive messages. In the field of speech and language pathology, fluency refers to the smoothness or flow with which sounds, syllables, words, and phrases are connected during speech. Fluency disorders encompass conditions such as cluttering and stuttering. Both of these disorders are characterized by disruptions in the fluidity of speech, often involving the repetition of parts of speech. These disorders are typically complex in nature and are observed more frequently in boys than in girls. Language fluency pertains to proficiency in a language, often a foreign or second language. This concept of fluency includes several distinct but interrelated skills: Reading: The ability to effortlessly read and comprehend texts written in the language. Writing: The capacity to construct written texts in the language. Comprehension: The skill to understand and follow spoken language. Speaking: The ability to articulate thoughts in the language and be understood by native speakers. These skills can be acquired independently to some extent. However, it is generally more challenging to develop auditory comprehension and fluent speaking abilities when learning a foreign language later in life. In contrast, reading and writing skills in a foreign language are often easier to acquire after the critical period for primary language acquisition has passed. Reading fluency, while related to language fluency, specifically refers to the ability to read text both accurately and quickly. It serves as a bridge between word decoding and comprehension, which is the understanding of the material being read. Reading fluency involves a set of skills that enable readers to decode text rapidly while maintaining a high level of comprehension. According to the National Reading Panel (2001), a key milestone in reading fluency is the ability to sight-read certain words. This means that children can instantly recognize the most common words in their native language's written form, which facilitates faster reading and comprehension of text. As children develop their reading abilities, the speed at which they read becomes an important metric. The National Reading Panel emphasizes that teaching children to read involves evidence-based strategies to enhance their fluency, comprehension, and overall reading proficiency.
